chunks.text: Op-ed · June 7, twenty twenty-six · 7 min read · By Don Goldstein

On July 1, DC's minimum wage steps to 18.40 dollars and the tipped base to 10.30 dollars. The number on the poster is small; the number on your P&L depends on what you do in the weeks before it lands.
In short
On July 1, twenty twenty-six, DC's minimum wage rises to 18.40 dollars and the tipped base to 10.30 dollars (56% of the full minimum).
Initiative 82 no longer eliminates the tip credit — DC capped it in twenty twenty-five at 75% of the minimum by twenty thirty-four, so the credit stays.
Absorb the step with a disclosed service charge, a 3-5% menu lift, or menu re-engineering; doing nothing reads as a margin slide by August.

On July 1, twenty twenty-six, the wage floor under every DC restaurant moves. The standard minimum rises to 18.40 dollars an hour, and the tipped base steps from 10.00 dollars to 10.30 dollars — now pegged at 56% of the full minimum. The number on the poster is small. The number on your prime cost depends entirely on what you do in the weeks before it lands.
Before the math, one correction — because half the operators I talk to have it backwards.
Initiative 82 is not eliminating the tip credit anymore.

That was the original plan when voters passed it. It changed. In July twenty twenty-five the DC Council amended Initiative 82: instead of phasing the tip credit to zero, the tipped wage is now capped — it rises toward 75% of the full minimum by twenty thirty-four, then holds. The tip credit stays, permanently. For July 1 that means your tipped base goes to 10.30 dollars and you still top up to 18.40 dollars in any week tips fall short. It is a step, not the cliff the original initiative pointed at.

What changes on your DC payroll on July first. One: the standard minimum wage rises from seventeen ninety-five to eighteen forty, for all employers. Two: the tipped base wage rises from ten dollars to ten thirty, now fifty-six percent of the full minimum. Three: the tip credit stays — DC capped Initiative 82 in twenty twenty-five, so the credit holds and rises toward seventy-five percent of the minimum by twenty thirty-four, rather than being eliminated.
The math you actually run.

The delta is smaller than the headlines and bigger than you think, depending on your mix. For tipped staff, the base moves 30 cents an hour — multiply by your weekly tipped hours and that is the floor of it. The real exposure is non-tipped labor — dish, prep, the line — anyone under 18.40 dollars moves up to it, and everyone stacked just above gets compressed. Run it on your own numbers in margin math rather than guessing; the point is to know the weekly figure before July, not to find it in the August labor line.
Three ways to absorb it — and the one that backfires.

Three ways to absorb the July first wage step, and one that backfires. One: a clearly disclosed service charge converts the raise into a line the guest sees, not a margin you eat. Two: a small menu lift, three to five percent on the right items, usually clears it without denting covers. Three: re-engineer the mix — push the high-margin items the menu already has. The one that backfires: absorbing it quietly, which reads as a one-to-two-point margin slide by August, after you have lost the window to price for it.
The 25 dollars question on the horizon.

There is a second clock. A coalition led by One Fair Wage filed a ballot measure in December twenty twenty-five to raise DC’s minimum to 25 dollars and eliminate the tip credit entirely; it cleared its subject review and is now collecting the signatures it needs to reach the November ballot. It is not law, and it may not qualify — but the operators who build the pricing muscle for the 18.40 dollars step are the ones who won’t be caught flat if the bigger number ever lands. Your average check , your cover count, and a disclosed service model are the levers either way.
July 1 is the small one. Treat it as the rehearsal.
Key takeaways
The standard minimum is 18.40 dollars and the tipped base 10.30 dollars on July 1, twenty twenty-six — non-tipped staff under 18.40 dollars drive most of the exposure.
The tip credit is capped, not eliminated; the twenty twenty-five amendment reversed Initiative 82's original phase-out.
A proposed 25 dollars ballot measure is collecting signatures — it is not law and may not qualify.
Price for the step before July; the window closes the day it lands.
